authoredVia: Signed-in ChatGPT in the in-app browser, one named theory section at a time

questions.question: Which description best explains a programmable lamp?
options: A timber object that must have a painted surface
A light, electronic system, code and physical design combined into one solution
An acrylic decoration without electronic components
A standard lamp that cannot be controlled
questions.correctFeedback: The project brings together physical construction, lighting, electronics, code and design.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Revisit the opening explanation and identify all four areas that contribute to the complete solution.

questions.question: Which category considers whether the lamp performs as intended?
options: Aesthetics
Construction
Function
Materials identification
questions.correctFeedback: Function considers whether the completed solution performs as intended.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish what the lamp does from how it looks or how carefully it is constructed.

questions.question: Which feature belongs mainly to aesthetics?
options: Shape and light effects
Exact circuitry
Workshop permission
Pin assignments
questions.correctFeedback: Shape, size, materials, finish and light effects contribute to the lamp’s aesthetics.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the features that affect the lamp’s visual appearance rather than its technical instructions.

questions.question: Which item is identified as an electronics component?
options: Tri-square
Radiata pine
Tenon saw
Arduino Uno board
questions.correctFeedback: The Arduino Uno board is named in the electronics-components section of the worksheet.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate electronic components from marking tools, cutting tools and construction materials.

questions.question: Why must the lamp’s materials, electronics and code be considered together?
options: They all perform the same role
They remove the need for design decisions
They can be selected without considering function
They contribute to one complete solution
questions.correctFeedback: The lamp works as an integrated solution, so decisions in one area can affect the others.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Revisit how physical design, lighting, electronics and code contribute to the same solution.

questions.question: Which material is specified as 3 mm thick?
options: Clear acrylic
Radiata pine
Solder
Jumper wire
questions.correctFeedback: The worksheet specifically identifies 3 mm clear acrylic.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Review the manufactured-material entry and look for the only stated material thickness.

questions.question: Which area is concerned mainly with the accuracy and care of the physical making?
options: Aesthetics
Programming syntax
Image resolution
Construction and build quality
questions.correctFeedback: Construction and build quality focus on how accurately and carefully the physical product is made.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the quality of physical making from appearance, coding rules and digital-image detail.

questions.question: Which action best communicates and evaluates a design idea?
options: Naming a component without explaining its role
Explaining design choices and comparing them with clear criteria
Copying the first idea without comparison
Listing tools in alphabetical order
questions.correctFeedback: Clear communication explains the choices made, while evaluation compares the idea with stated criteria.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the action that both explains the idea and judges it against something checkable.

questions.question: Which statement is the most useful success criterion?
options: The lamp should be good
The design should use every possible material
The first idea should be accepted
The finished result can be checked against a clearly stated requirement
questions.correctFeedback: A useful criterion states something observable that can be checked when the solution is evaluated.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the statement that gives a clear basis for checking the finished solution.

questions.question: What should a student do when a component relationship or practical detail is unclear?
options: Guess from a similar project
Choose the most convenient connection
Treat the component list as a complete procedure
Record the uncertainty and verify the detail before proceeding
questions.correctFeedback: Recording and verifying an unknown prevents an unsupported assumption from becoming part of the project.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the response that protects accuracy by resolving missing information before practical work.

sections.title: Workshop safety: hazards, risk controls and responsibility

questions.question: What is a hazard?
options: The possible seriousness of an injury
A source or situation that could cause harm
A completed safety record
A control used to reduce risk
questions.correctFeedback: A hazard is something with the potential to cause injury or other harm.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the thing that could cause harm from the risk it creates and the control used to reduce it.

questions.question: When may a student use the fixed disc sander?
options: Whenever the machine is free
After watching another student use it
Only after required training, a passed safety test, permission and demonstrated safe use
After reading one warning label
questions.correctFeedback: All required training, testing, permission and safe-use conditions must be met before operation.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the complete safety-authorisation process, not one isolated step.

questions.question: What should a student do after noticing faulty equipment?
options: Keep using it carefully
Try to repair it
Leave it for the next person
Stop using it and report the fault immediately
questions.correctFeedback: Faulty equipment must be taken out of use and reported immediately.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Do not test, repair or ignore equipment that may be unsafe.

questions.question: What must happen before the fixed disc sander is adjusted or cleaned?
options: The guard is removed
The work is held against the disc
The machine is switched off and completely stopped
A second student enters the machine zone
questions.correctFeedback: The machine must be switched off and fully stopped before adjustment or cleaning.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the control that removes machine movement before another task begins.

questions.question: Why does good workshop organisation matter?
options: It replaces PPE
It reduces avoidable hazards and supports safe movement
It makes training unnecessary
It allows damaged tools to remain in use
questions.correctFeedback: A clean, organised workspace reduces avoidable hazards but still works alongside other safety controls.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Organisation supports safe work; it does not replace PPE, training or equipment checks.

questions.question: How many students may be in the fixed disc-sander machine zone while it is being used?
options: Two
Three
Any number wearing eye protection
One
questions.correctFeedback: Only one student may be in the machine zone while the disc sander is being used.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The machine-zone rule limits the space to the single operator.

questions.question: Which group contains only risks associated with the fixed disc sander?
options: Sunburn, dehydration and traffic
Eye injury, abrasion, burns, entanglement and dust inhalation
Chemical spills, radiation and flooding
Noise from music, glare and wet weather
questions.correctFeedback: The identified disc-sander risks include eye injury, abrasion, burns, entanglement and dust inhalation.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the group connected directly to contact, moving parts and sanding dust.

questions.question: What should a student do after noticing unsafe behaviour in the workshop?
options: Join in so the person stops
Ignore it until the end of the lesson
Move clear of the danger and report it immediately
Post a warning online
questions.correctFeedback: Moving clear and reporting the behaviour promptly helps prevent harm.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the response that addresses the danger immediately without increasing it.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a safe operating procedure (SOP)?
options: It replaces practical training
It guarantees that every hazard has been removed
It gives permission to improvise with equipment
It supports training and other safety controls
questions.correctFeedback: An SOP supports safe work but must be used with training, permission and local controls.
questions.incorrectFeedback: An SOP is an important control, but it does not remove the need for the other controls.

questions.question: What does personal responsibility in the workshop include?
options: Using unfamiliar equipment when others are busy
Following controls, wearing required PPE and reporting hazards
Repairing faults without training
Leaving housekeeping to another student
questions.correctFeedback: Personal responsibility means making safe choices and responding properly to hazards each lesson.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the actions that each student can control and that reduce risk.

sections.title: Measurement, scale and reading the supplied drawing

questions.question: Why does the project commonly use millimetres?
options: Millimetres remove the need for drawings
The laser cutter uses millimetres for precision
Workshop rulers show metres only
Millimetres make every view full size
questions.correctFeedback: The measurement worksheet identifies millimetres as the precision unit used by the laser cutter.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Review which unit is linked specifically to precise digital fabrication in the measurement worksheet.

questions.question: Which conversion is correct?
options: 10 mm = 10 cm
questions.correctFeedback: One thousand millimetres and one hundred centimetres both equal one metre.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Compare the verified relationships between millimetres, centimetres and metres before selecting an equivalent value.

questions.question: How should a measurement taken with a workshop ruler be recorded?
options: As a screen percentage
Without a unit
In millimetres
Only as a rough fraction
questions.correctFeedback: Recording the value in millimetres keeps the measurement precise and unambiguous.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the unit identified for ruler measurements in this project.

questions.question: What does a written dimension on a technical drawing represent?
options: The size of the image on the current screen
The distance measured from any photocopy
The preferred printer setting
The intended real size
questions.correctFeedback: Written dimensions communicate the intended real measurement, regardless of how the page is displayed.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the designed size of the object from the temporary size of its printed or onscreen representation.

questions.question: What does a view scale of 1:2 mean?
options: The intended printed view is half the real size
The object must be made twice
Every dimension must be divided by two
The view is intended to be full size
questions.correctFeedback: A 1:2 view represents the object at half its intended real size on the drawing.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about the relationship between one unit on the view and two corresponding units on the real object.

questions.question: Why should students not measure a dimension directly from a computer screen?
options: Screens cannot display technical drawings
Every drawing number is shown in metres
The displayed page may have been resized
Scale applies only to handwritten sketches
questions.correctFeedback: Screen zoom and page resizing can change the displayed size without changing the written dimension.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider whether the visual size of a document remains fixed across different screens and zoom levels.

questions.question: Which scale is shown on the two detail views?
questions.correctFeedback: Two detail views on the authorised drawing are explicitly labelled “SCALE 1:1”.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish the scale beside the detail views from the overall scale shown in the title block.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the three written sequence notes?
options: Cut first; cut second; sand third
Sand first; cut second; cut third
Cut first and sand; cut third; cut second and sand
Cut first and sand; cut second and sand; cut third
questions.correctFeedback: This matches the numbered sequence written on the authorised drawing.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Follow the numbers from one to three and preserve the sanding words attached to each note.

questions.question: What should a student do before assigning a dimension to a feature?
options: Follow its arrows and extension lines in the correct view
Choose the nearest visible number
Measure the feature from the screen
Assume matching-looking features are identical
questions.correctFeedback: Dimension lines and the relevant view help establish which feature the written value describes.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the drawing information that connects a number to a particular location rather than relying on proximity.

questions.question: What should a student do when a dimension or feature relationship is unclear?
options: Estimate it from the screen preview
Record the uncertainty and clarify it before marking or cutting
Copy a value from a different view
Choose the smallest visible number
questions.correctFeedback: Unclear drawing information must be resolved before it is used for practical work.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Do not assign a number to a feature until the relationship has been checked.

sections.title: Image quality, resolution and design research

questions.question: What is the main purpose of image research in design?
options: To avoid developing original ideas
To collect references and compare possible ideas
To guarantee that an image can be manufactured
To select the first image found
questions.correctFeedback: Research provides visual evidence that can support idea generation, comparison and explanation.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on how research supports several possible ideas rather than immediately deciding on one final image.

questions.question: What does image resolution describe?
options: Whether an image is legally available
The physical size of the lamp
The pixel dimensions of the image
The number of design ideas required
questions.correctFeedback: Resolution is commonly recorded as an image’s pixel width by pixel height.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the digital detail information of an image from its ownership, design purpose or manufactured size.

questions.question: Why might an image look sharp when small but poor when enlarged?
options: Its available pixel detail becomes more visible when enlarged
Every enlarged image becomes a vector automatically
Its title changes when resized
Enlarging confirms its copyright status
questions.correctFeedback: Enlarging an image can expose limited pixel detail as blur or blockiness.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about what happens to the visible digital detail when the same pixels are spread across a larger display area.

questions.question: Which information should be recorded for a useful research image?
options: Only its colour
Only the website name
Only its resolution
Its source, title or subject, resolution and design relevance
questions.correctFeedback: These details make the reference easier to identify, compare and explain later.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the option that records both where the image came from and why it may help the design process.

questions.question: What does design relevance explain?
options: Whether the image has the highest pixel count
What the image contributes to the student’s design thinking
Which machine will manufacture the lamp
Whether the image is automatically approved
questions.correctFeedback: Design relevance links the reference to useful features such as shape, outline or arrangement.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the reason the image is useful as a reference, not on technical approval or machine operation.

questions.question: Why should a designer compare several reference images before choosing a direction?
options: To guarantee that every image can be copied
To remove the need for design criteria
To make resolution irrelevant
To avoid selecting too early and to justify later choices
questions.correctFeedback: Comparing several references reveals different possibilities and provides evidence for a reasoned choice.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about how comparison improves a design decision rather than merely increasing the number of images.

questions.question: How should an example design influence a student’s own idea?
options: It can suggest strategies that are adapted into an original response
It should be copied exactly
It should be treated as the required theme
It should decide the final colours automatically
questions.correctFeedback: An example can prompt thinking, but the student must develop and justify an original response.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use an example as inspiration and evidence for comparison, not as a compulsory design.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a research image and a final vector design?
options: They are always identical
Any research image is ready for laser cutting
A vector design is unnecessary when resolution is high
The reference informs thinking, while the final vector must be developed and checked separately
questions.correctFeedback: Inspiration and manufacturing information serve different stages of the design process.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider whether finding an image completes the work needed to prepare a controlled manufacturing design.
questions.source: Drive file IDs 1VmOGpI0qTXPmWWKYMRD8ewtJcGRQB1kpf_zQNSFwppQ and 1xBOBGVdnWhorJVeTTqZPw5yRNeWkF249; NESA TE4-PDP-01

questions.question: Why is vector-design practice useful before developing a final lamp graphic?
options: It proves any downloaded image can be manufactured
It supplies the lamp’s final dimensions
It develops skills with outlines, layers and simplification
It removes the need to compare ideas
questions.correctFeedback: Practice with outlines, layers and simple shapes builds transferable vector-design skills.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the design skills being developed, not on unrelated lamp specifications.

questions.question: What should be checked before using a reference image in a design?
options: Its source, reuse permission, resolution and design relevance
Only whether it looks colourful
Whether it was the first search result
Whether it already contains a finished lamp
questions.correctFeedback: Responsible design research checks where an image came from, whether it may be reused, its quality and its relevance.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the combination that checks both responsible use and design usefulness.
questions.source: Drive file IDs 1VmOGpI0qTXPmWWKYMRD8ewtJcGRQB1kpf_zQNSFwppQ and 1OmW9UvXZ44MtOGNVmq7THl65bglDtKBwJ4exdkAqWF8; NESA TE4-DIG-01

sections.title: Vector design: outlines, layers and laser-ready simplicity

questions.question: What does a vector design use to describe shapes?
options: Editable lines and curves
A fixed grid of timber dimensions
Electronic pin assignments
A photograph’s colour settings
questions.correctFeedback: Vector designs are built from editable paths rather than relying on a fixed pixel grid.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on how the digital shape is constructed, not on project materials, circuitry or photographic settings.
questions.source: Week 3 Drive PDF ID 1xBOBGVdnWhorJVeTTqZPw5yRNeWkF249; NESA TE4-DIG-02

questions.question: What belongs on the base layer of the two-layer practice design?
options: Added text or small details
The main outline
A pixel-based reference image
A written evaluation
questions.correctFeedback: The base layer contains the main outline that establishes the overall shape.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the main shape from the smaller details added on the second layer.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Layer 2 in the practice activity?
options: To set the final lamp dimensions
To approve the design for manufacture
To add details such as text or smaller shapes
To control the RGB LED strip
questions.correctFeedback: The second layer holds added details that sit above or within the base design.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the layer used to organise visual details rather than project dimensions, approval or electronics.

questions.question: Why is simplicity useful in a vector design?
options: It guarantees a perfect manufactured result
It turns a pixel image into a vector automatically
It makes paths easier to inspect, edit and understand
It makes layers unnecessary
questions.correctFeedback: Removing unnecessary detail makes the paths and intended result easier to inspect and communicate.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider how complexity affects editing, inspection and clarity.
questions.source: Week 3 Drive PDF ID 1xBOBGVdnWhorJVeTTqZPw5yRNeWkF249; NESA TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Why should design constraints such as maximum size be checked before export?
options: To guarantee every outline is closed
To select a programming language
To determine the timber species
To ensure the design fits the stated brief and avoid preventable rework
questions.correctFeedback: Checking constraints before export helps ensure the design meets the brief before it moves to the next stage.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the reason connected to meeting the design requirements, not another project area.

questions.question: What should be checked about an outline before export?
options: Whether it is closed where intended
Whether it matches the lamp circuitry
Whether it uses the approved laser setting
Whether it includes six colours
questions.correctFeedback: Students should inspect whether outlines are complete and whether any open path is deliberate.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on path quality within the vector file rather than circuitry, machine settings or invented colour requirements.
questions.source: Week 3 Drive PDF ID 1xBOBGVdnWhorJVeTTqZPw5yRNeWkF249; NESA TE4-PPM-01

questions.question: Which features make a vector design ready for checking?
options: A large number of decorative points
A hidden base outline
An unedited pixel photograph
Clear layers, deliberate paths and readable details
questions.correctFeedback: Clear organisation and deliberate paths make the design easier to inspect before manufacturing decisions are made.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the combination that makes the vector structure clear and intentional.
questions.source: Week 3 Drive PDF ID 1xBOBGVdnWhorJVeTTqZPw5yRNeWkF249; NESA TE4-PPM-01

questions.question: How do layers make a vector design easier to edit?
options: They convert every shape into a photograph
They lock all paths permanently
They separate the base outline from added details
They remove the need for an outline
questions.correctFeedback: Separating the base and details allows each part to be inspected and changed without confusing the whole design.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about how organising different design elements supports precise editing.
questions.source: Week 3 Drive PDF ID 1xBOBGVdnWhorJVeTTqZPw5yRNeWkF249; NESA TE4-PDP-01

questions.question: Why can a high-resolution photograph not automatically be treated as a finished vector design?
options: High-resolution images contain no visual detail
Resolution describes pixels, while a vector requires deliberate editable paths
Photographs always have two vector layers
Resolution fixes all manufacturing decisions
questions.correctFeedback: A detailed pixel image may be useful research, but a vector design still needs clear, intentional lines and curves.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate pixel detail from the editable paths used to describe vector shapes.

questions.question: Which change best reduces unnecessary vector complexity?
options: Removing redundant detail while keeping the form recognisable
Adding more points to every curve
Duplicating small decorative shapes
Merging the base and details without checking them
questions.correctFeedback: Removing redundant detail can make paths clearer while preserving the intended form.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the change that simplifies the design without losing its essential idea.

sections.title: Iterating ideas and building success criteria

questions.question: What does iteration mean in the design process?
options: Repeating a process so each cycle builds towards a desired result
Manufacturing every idea that is generated
Selecting the first idea that appears suitable
Copying the same drawing without changes
questions.correctFeedback: Iteration uses repeated cycles of development to move towards a more suitable design result.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on purposeful improvement between cycles rather than simple repetition or immediate manufacture.

questions.question: What should each design idea include to support later comparison?
options: A complete production schedule
A finished electronic circuit
A final product judgement
A reference or context and an explanation of its design relevance
questions.correctFeedback: An explained idea shows both what influenced it and how that influence may contribute to the lamp.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for information that makes the idea understandable and comparable.

questions.question: What is the best way to use another student’s example during idea development?
options: Copy its theme and colours
Identify useful strategies, then develop an original response
Treat it as the required final solution
Skip further research
questions.correctFeedback: Examples can demonstrate a process or strategy without becoming a design requirement.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the example to extend your thinking, not to replace your own idea development.

questions.question: Why should students generate several explained ideas?
options: To prove every idea can be manufactured
To avoid evaluating design features
To make all ideas look identical
To compare possibilities before choosing or refining features
questions.correctFeedback: Several explained ideas provide evidence for comparison and more deliberate design decisions.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider how multiple alternatives reduce the risk of choosing too early without comparison.

questions.question: Which category considers whether the solution performs as intended?
options: Function
Aesthetics
Personal goal
Image resolution
questions.correctFeedback: Function considers whether the designed solution carries out its intended purpose.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish performance from appearance, individual improvement and research-image quality.

questions.question: Which statement is the most useful description of a success criterion?
options: It names a favourite logo
It describes something observable that can be checked later
It records only a student’s personal preference
It guarantees the design will be manufactured
questions.correctFeedback: Observable criteria give students a practical basis for evaluating the completed solution.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for wording that can guide later evaluation rather than preference, prediction or automatic approval.

questions.question: What may students do with a feature during iteration?
options: Retain, refine, combine or reject it for a stated reason
Use it without comparing it to any criteria
Manufacture it before discussing constraints
Treat it as compulsory because it appears in a reference image
questions.correctFeedback: Iteration requires purposeful decisions supported by comparison and explanation.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on evidence-based design decisions rather than automatic acceptance or premature manufacture.
questions.source: NESA glossary meaning of iteration; NESA TE4-PDP-01 and TE4-DES-01

questions.question: What is the relationship between a personal goal and a project criterion?
options: They are always the same statement
A personal goal automatically applies to the whole class
A personal goal concerns one student, while a criterion applies to the solution
Project criteria are optional once a personal goal is chosen
questions.correctFeedback: The two statements serve different purposes within the project.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Compare who or what each statement is intended to guide and evaluate.

questions.question: What do the image-search records contribute to idea iteration?
options: Confirmed lamp manufacturing dimensions
Reference images and resolution information for research
Final class constraints
Approved machine procedures
questions.correctFeedback: The task supports research evidence, not final technical or manufacturing decisions.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish visual research information from dimensions, constraints and workshop procedures.

questions.question: Why should success criteria be recorded before the final solution is evaluated?
options: They provide a consistent basis for judging the result
They guarantee that the first design will work
They remove the need to gather evidence
They decide which idea every student must choose
questions.correctFeedback: Recorded criteria give the evaluation a clear and consistent standard for comparison.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the reason that connects criteria with fair, evidence-based evaluation.

sections.title: Hardwood, softwood and a reasoned material choice

questions.question: What do the terms hardwood and softwood mainly describe?
options: Guaranteed timber strength
Botanical timber groups
The price of the timber
The required surface finish
questions.correctFeedback: These terms classify timber by botanical origin rather than guaranteeing its physical hardness.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the timber’s classification from properties such as strength, cost and surface condition.

questions.question: Which statement about softwood is correct?
options: It is wood from conifers such as pine
It is always softer than every hardwood
It must come from native forest
It always has the same grain pattern
questions.correctFeedback: Softwood is classified as wood from conifers, regardless of its actual physical softness.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the botanical definition rather than an unsupported claim about hardness, source or appearance.

questions.question: Why does the name “softwood” not prove actual softness?
options: Timber names are selected by students
Softwood refers only to timber colour
The category is anatomical and exceptions occur
Every softwood is manufactured material
questions.correctFeedback: The classification commonly, but not always, corresponds with softer or lighter timber.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider whether a botanical category can guarantee one physical property in every species and piece.

questions.question: Which timber is named for the Programmable Lamp project?
options: Tasmanian oak
Blackbutt
Hoop pine
Radiata pine
questions.correctFeedback: Radiata pine appears in the authorised Tool and Materials Identification Worksheet.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Return to the project material list rather than choosing another Australian timber example.

questions.question: How is radiata pine classified?
options: As a softwood
As a hardwood
As an acrylic
As a timber finish
questions.correctFeedback: Radiata pine belongs to the pine group and is classified as a softwood.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Apply the botanical definition of softwood to the named project timber.
questions.source: Drive file ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg; Australian Government DAFF forestry glossary

questions.question: Which factor should contribute to a reasoned material choice?
options: Whether the timber has the shortest name
Whether another student prefers it
Its intended function and verified properties
Whether it is labelled hardwood
questions.correctFeedback: Material selection should connect reliable evidence about the timber to the solution’s intended function.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the factor that links evidence about the material to what the product must do.

questions.question: Why is the label hardwood or softwood insufficient on its own when choosing timber?
options: Both groups always have identical properties
The label gives the exact stock dimensions
The botanical group does not prove the timber’s actual hardness, cost or suitability
The label proves the source is sustainable
questions.correctFeedback: Botanical classification is useful, but a material choice also needs evidence about the actual timber and intended function.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Do not treat a timber group name as proof of every property or project requirement.

questions.question: What is a plantation forest?
options: Any group of trees beside a workshop
Only a naturally occurring native forest
A collection of timber stored for sale
An intentionally established and managed stand of trees
questions.correctFeedback: Plantation forests are deliberately established and managed, including for commercial wood production.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on how the forest stand is established and managed rather than where processed timber is stored.

questions.question: Which claim should a student avoid without supporting evidence?
options: Radiata pine is named in the project worksheet
Pine is classified as softwood
All softwoods are cheaper and easier to work
Material choice should consider intended function
questions.correctFeedback: The sources do not prove that every softwood shares the same cost or workability.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Find the statement that turns a botanical category into an unsupported universal property claim.

questions.question: Which evidence would strengthen a judgement about radiata pine for the lamp base?
options: The assumption that all softwoods are cheap
Its relevant properties, workability, appearance, availability and sustainability evidence
The name softwood by itself
A preference unrelated to the lamp’s function
questions.correctFeedback: A reasoned choice links verified material evidence to the intended function of the lamp base.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose evidence about the actual material and its use, not a broad timber stereotype.

sections.title: Native forests, plantations and sustainable choices

questions.question: What best describes a native forest?
options: A stand planted only for commercial timber
A forest dominated by native species associated with that location
Any forest containing one native tree
A forest that can never be harvested
questions.correctFeedback: Native forests are defined by native tree species occurring within their natural location and range.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the species and their natural relationship to the location, not on one management decision.

questions.question: What is a plantation?
options: An intensively managed stand established by placing seedlings or seeds
Any naturally regenerated native forest
A timber storage area beside a sawmill
A forest that contains only softwood trees
questions.correctFeedback: Plantations are deliberately established stands and may contain native or exotic tree species.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the definition based on deliberate establishment and management rather than species type alone.

questions.question: What are commercial plantations managed to produce?
options: Only wildlife habitat
Finished furniture
Wood for commercial production
Unmanaged natural regeneration
questions.correctFeedback: Commercial plantations are managed to supply logs used in producing wood products.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish growing and supplying timber from manufacturing a finished product.

questions.question: Why does the label “plantation timber” not automatically prove sustainability?
options: Plantations never contain trees
All plantations use identical management
Sustainability applies only to native forests
Evidence about management, harvesting and regeneration is still required
questions.correctFeedback: Forest type alone does not reveal all environmental, social and production effects.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider what additional evidence is needed beyond knowing how the forest was established.

questions.question: Which information is useful when judging a timber source?
options: Origin, management and regeneration evidence
Whether its name sounds environmentally friendly
Whether another student selected it
The colour of the worksheet
questions.correctFeedback: These details help evaluate how timber production may affect environments and future supply.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose evidence that explains where the timber came from and what happens before and after harvesting.

questions.question: Which statement about native forest harvesting is supported?
options: It is always environmentally harmless
Its effects depend on location, management and protections
It is automatically less sustainable than every plantation
It occurs without environmental regulation
questions.correctFeedback: A balanced judgement requires evidence about the particular operation and its management context.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Avoid absolute claims and consider how the consequences may vary between locations and management systems.

questions.question: Which is an ecological value supported by forests?
options: Automatic product certification
Guaranteed low timber prices
Soil and water protection
Identical timber properties
questions.correctFeedback: Forests contribute to protecting soil and water as well as supporting ecosystems and biodiversity.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify the environmental function rather than a commercial or material claim unsupported by forest type.

questions.question: What should students separate when comparing timber sources?
options: Tree colour from timber length
Project work from classroom discussion
Sustainability from evidence
Forest type from management and harvesting decisions
questions.correctFeedback: A forest category does not fully explain how a particular area is managed or harvested.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about the difference between what a forest is and what people decide to do within it.

questions.question: Which conclusion is most defensible when comparing native-forest and plantation timber?
options: One forest type is always sustainable
All native-forest harvesting is harmful
Sustainability depends on evidence about origin, management, regeneration and impacts
All plantation timber has no environmental effects
questions.correctFeedback: Forest type alone does not determine sustainability; management evidence and impacts must also be considered.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Avoid absolute claims and choose the conclusion supported by several kinds of evidence.

questions.question: Which evidence would best support a sustainable timber-sourcing decision?
options: Origin, management, protection, regeneration and relevant impacts
A forest-type label alone
The colour of the timber
A claim that every source is equivalent
questions.correctFeedback: A sustainable sourcing decision needs evidence about where the timber came from and how the forest is managed over time.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look beyond a single label to the evidence that explains long-term effects.

sections.title: Planning timber production from drawing to evidence

questions.question: What should be the starting point for a timber production plan?
options: A sequence remembered from another project
Confirmed evidence from the supplied drawing
The tools currently available on a bench
An assumed method for making a lamp base
questions.correctFeedback: A production plan should begin with verified drawing information rather than habits or assumptions from unrelated work.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify which option comes directly from the authorised project information before any practical method is proposed.
questions.source: Programmable Lamp drawing, Drive ID 1I5PiH8vw7PerhH0PgMeWYkltm6z1rVNZ; TE4-PPM-01

questions.question: What does the overall scale of 1:2 describe?
options: The view is presented at half the intended real size
Every written dimension must be divided by two
Two identical lamp bases must be produced
The timber is twice its required thickness
questions.correctFeedback: Scale describes the relationship between the displayed view and the real object, not a change to written dimensions.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the printed size of the view from the real-size information communicated by written dimensions.

Sand first, cut second, cut third
Cut first and sand, cut second and sand, cut third
Cut third, cut first and sand, cut second and sand

questions.question: What should a student do when a production feature or measurement is unclear?

Copy a number from an unrelated view
Add a new dimension to the drawing
Record the uncertainty and clarify it before practical work
questions.correctFeedback: Unclear information must be resolved before it is turned into a practical instruction.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the action that keeps the plan accurate without inventing missing detail.
questions.source: Programmable Lamp drawing, Drive ID 1I5PiH8vw7PerhH0PgMeWYkltm6z1rVNZ; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Which timber must the production plan account for when planning the lamp base?
options: Jarrah
Blackbutt
Balsa
Radiata pine

questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the named project timber rather than substituting another species.
questions.source: Tool & Materials Identification Worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg

questions.question: What should be matched before selecting a tool for a production step?
options: The tool colour and storage shelf
The number of photos already taken
The operation, material and required safety controls
The design theme only

questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the factors that determine whether the tool is suitable and safe for the task.
questions.source: Tool & Materials Identification Worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg; TE4-SAF-01

questions.question: Which action is an appropriate pre-production checkpoint?
options: Inventing a tolerance for each dimension
Selecting machine settings from memory
Confirming the drawing title, scale, view and units
Completing an unverified sawmill sequence
questions.correctFeedback: These checks use available drawing and measurement evidence without adding unsupported manufacturing information.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the checkpoint that verifies supplied information rather than inventing missing technical details.

questions.question: Which item could provide useful production evidence?
options: An undocumented change made during practical work
A guessed dimension written after production

questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for evidence that records the authorised process clearly rather than disguising assumptions or changes.

questions.question: How is a project production plan different from a general sawmill process?
options: It describes only how logs become commercial timber
It translates the specific product drawing into organised making and checking steps
It ignores dimensions and checkpoints
It automatically supplies every machine setting

questions.question: What makes a production plan useful before work begins?
options: It organises drawing evidence, a proposed sequence, checkpoints and unresolved details
It permits every machine to be used
It replaces all safe operating procedures
It turns estimates into exact dimensions
questions.correctFeedback: A useful plan organises what is known and clearly identifies what still needs clarification.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the purpose of planning rather than treating the plan as permission or a substitute for safety controls.

sections.title: Coding language: algorithms, sequencing and syntax

questions.question: What is coding?
options: Measuring electronic components
Writing instructions in a programming language
Drawing the lamp base
Connecting any available hardware
questions.correctFeedback: Coding communicates instructions that a digital system can follow to produce an intended behaviour.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the activity involving written digital instructions rather than construction or hardware assembly.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k

questions.question: What is an algorithm?
options: A clear set of steps for completing a task
A confirmed hardware circuit
A type of USB cable
A programming error
questions.correctFeedback: An algorithm organises the actions needed to reach a result before language-specific coding begins.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the option describing an ordered method rather than equipment or a fault.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k; TE4-DIG-02

questions.question: Why can an algorithm be written before a programming language is confirmed?
options: Algorithms contain approved pin numbers
Every language uses identical syntax
Algorithms can describe steps in human-readable language
Algorithms automatically operate hardware

questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate a general explanation of steps from instructions written for a particular digital system.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: What does sequencing involve?
options: Selecting a timber species
Naming electronic components
Correcting the lamp drawing scale
Arranging instructions in the intended order

questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify the concept concerned with order rather than materials, hardware names or drawing information.

questions.question: Why can changing an instruction sequence affect the result?
options: Instructions may occur at different stages or in the wrong order
The Arduino Uno changes into another component
The programming language becomes unnecessary
The drawing scale changes automatically
questions.correctFeedback: Digital behaviour depends on instructions being carried out in an order that matches the intended process.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider how changing which action occurs first or next could alter the planned behaviour.

questions.question: What is syntax?
options: The physical arrangement of jumper wires
The rules for writing instructions in a particular programming language
The visible colour of the lamp
The order of timber production
questions.correctFeedback: Syntax controls how words, symbols and structures must be written in the selected language.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for rules governing written code rather than physical construction or design appearance.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an algorithm from code?
options: An algorithm must use the final programming syntax
Code can be written without any language
An algorithm describes steps, while code translates them into a programming language
They are always identical documents

questions.incorrectFeedback: Compare the planning description with its later translation into instructions for a digital system.

options: The timber’s botanical group
The programming language’s syntax and the hardware configuration
The image resolution
The lamp’s final evaluation

questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify the technical information needed to turn human-readable steps into executable instructions.

questions.question: A set of correct actions has been placed in a confusing order. Which coding concept needs improvement?
options: Resolution
Sustainability
Sequencing
Material classification
questions.correctFeedback: Sequencing arranges instructions in the order needed to produce the intended result.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the coding concept concerned with what happens first, next and last.
questions.source: Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg

questions.question: Which process best supports reviewing planned light behaviour?
options: Write code before deciding what should happen
Assume the hardware configuration from the component list
Skip the algorithm and test random instructions
Decide the behaviour, order the steps, then communicate and review them
questions.correctFeedback: This process allows the intended behaviour and sequence to be checked before technical translation begins.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Select the approach that plans and communicates the intended result before relying on unconfirmed technical details.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k; TE4-DES-01 and TE4-DIG-02

sections.title: Variables, loops and conditionals for light behaviour

questions.question: What is a variable used to represent?
options: A named value or piece of information that may change
A physical connection between components
A fixed drawing dimension
A workshop safety procedure
questions.correctFeedback: A variable allows changing information to be identified and used within an organised digital process.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on information handled by a program rather than physical construction or workshop instructions.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k; Official Arduino Language Reference

questions.question: What is the purpose of a loop?
options: To identify the hardware voltage
To select the project material
To repeat an instruction or group of instructions
To connect the RGB LED strip
questions.correctFeedback: A loop organises repeated behaviour without requiring the same planned action to be stated separately each time.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the concept concerned with repetition rather than hardware or material selection.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k

questions.question: What does a conditional do?
options: Repeats every instruction forever
Selects an action depending on whether a condition is met
Stores the project drawing
Confirms the programming language
questions.correctFeedback: A conditional supports controlled decision-making by linking possible actions to a stated condition.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish choosing between actions from repeating instructions or storing information.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes a variable from a loop?
options: A variable repeats actions, while a loop stores hardware
Both terms refer only to wiring
A loop stores changing values, while a variable selects actions
A variable represents information, while a loop organises repetition
questions.correctFeedback: The concepts have different roles: one represents information and the other controls repeated instructions.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Compare what each concept handles rather than treating them as interchangeable coding terms.

questions.question: A value representing the current light state may change while a program runs. Which concept represents that changing information?

A conditional
A vector path
A variable
questions.correctFeedback: A variable represents information that may change while a program operates.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the concept used to hold changing information, not repeat or select actions.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg

options: When an intended action needs to occur again
When stock dimensions need measuring
When a circuit must be invented
When the timber needs classifying

questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the situation involving repetition within digital behaviour rather than another project area.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k; TE4-DIG-02

questions.question: What must a conditional identify?
options: A condition and the action selected when it is met or not met
Only a repeated action
A timber species and grain pattern
A vector outline and layer name
questions.correctFeedback: A conditional makes a choice by testing a condition and selecting the corresponding action.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the structure that connects a test with alternative actions.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg; TE4-DIG-02

questions.question: What is the purpose of a stopping rule in a loop?
options: To store changing information
To choose the timber source
To define when repetition should end
To organise vector layers
questions.correctFeedback: A stopping rule controls when repeated actions finish instead of continuing indefinitely.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Separate the control of repetition from variables and unrelated project decisions.

questions.question: Before coding a light behaviour, what should the algorithm identify?
options: Only the final appearance
The forest-management method
Every machine setting
What information may change, what actions may repeat and what decisions are required
questions.correctFeedback: A language-neutral plan should identify the changing information, repetition and decisions that shape the intended behaviour.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the description that plans the behaviour before language-specific code is written.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01 and TE4-DIG-02

questions.question: Which combination correctly matches each coding concept with its purpose?
options: Variable—repeats actions; loop—selects a timber; conditional—draws vectors

Variable—controls layers; loop—stores images; conditional—measures timber
Variable—selects an action; loop—stores changing information; conditional—always repeats

Linking each decision to relevant evidence such as drawings, tests and design records
questions.correctFeedback: Traceable communication shows the evidence and reasoning behind each design decision.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the approach that lets another person follow where a decision came from.
questions.source: Lamp Idea Iteration, Drive ID 1OmW9UvXZ44MtOGNVmq7THl65bglDtKBwJ4exdkAqWF8; Programmable Lamp drawing, Drive ID 1I5PiH8vw7PerhH0PgMeWYkltm6z1rVNZ; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Why should interfaces be checked before final assembly?
options: Every interface is automatically compatible
Interfaces concern appearance only
A mismatch between parts can affect fit, function and the complete solution
Checking one part proves all other parts will work
questions.correctFeedback: Checking interfaces helps find compatibility problems before separate parts are treated as one finished system.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about how a problem where parts meet can affect the whole solution.
questions.source: Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg; Programmable Lamp drawing, Drive ID 1I5PiH8vw7PerhH0PgMeWYkltm6z1rVNZ

sections.title: Testing, debugging and improving the solution

questions.question: What is testing?
options: Changing several parts until the result looks better
Comparing an observed result with a confirmed criterion
Copying another student’s solution
Assuming the system works because it starts
questions.correctFeedback: Testing requires a known expectation, an observed result and a clear comparison between them.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the process that uses evidence to judge a result against an agreed expectation.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: What is debugging?
options: A systematic process of locating, explaining and correcting a fault
Replacing every component at once
Changing several settings without recording them
Selecting the lamp’s materials
questions.correctFeedback: Debugging uses an organised investigation rather than random changes.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the process used to explain why a system does not match expectations and correct it.
questions.source: What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k; TE4-DIG-02

questions.question: What should be stated before beginning a test?
options: A guessed fault
A preferred repair
The criterion being tested
A vague description such as ‘good’
questions.correctFeedback: The criterion provides the standard against which the observed result will be compared.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify the information needed to decide whether the test result meets the intended requirement.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-PPM-01

questions.question: Why should students predict the expected result?
options: To replace the need for observation
To guarantee that the test will pass
To select an unconfirmed circuit
To create a clear expectation for later comparison
questions.correctFeedback: A prediction helps students compare what they expected with what was actually observed.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Think about how an expected result helps organise the evidence collected after testing.

questions.question: Which action produces useful test evidence?
options: Recording the observed result
Relying on memory after several changes
Ignoring an unexpected result
Describing the outcome only as “good”
questions.correctFeedback: Recorded observations make the test traceable and allow later comparison with the criterion and prediction.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the action that preserves specific evidence rather than relying on memory or vague judgement.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Why group possible faults into areas such as design/material, connection/component and code/logic?
options: To organise a systematic investigation
To prove the cause before testing
To justify changing every part at once
To avoid recording observations
questions.correctFeedback: Diagnostic groups help organise possible causes so they can be investigated methodically.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The groups guide the investigation; they do not prove a cause by themselves.
questions.source: Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg; What is coding worksheet, Drive ID 1aEDElMGsxxIcAo-rCDUe49_leQwztNNdOh2PIEp_e2k

questions.question: Why should only one controlled element be changed at a time?
options: It guarantees every fault is fixed
It helps show whether that change affected the result
It makes observations unnecessary
It proves all settings are correct
questions.correctFeedback: A single controlled change makes cause-and-effect evidence easier to interpret.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider what happens to the evidence when several elements change together.
questions.source: Lamp Idea Iteration, Drive ID 1OmW9UvXZ44MtOGNVmq7THl65bglDtKBwJ4exdkAqWF8; TE4-PPM-01

questions.question: What should happen after one controlled element is changed?
options: Discard the earlier record
Change several more elements immediately
Replace the original criterion
Retest the same aspect and compare the result
questions.correctFeedback: Retesting the same aspect allows a fair comparison with the earlier evidence.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the step that checks whether the single change affected the original result.

questions.question: When can a change be described as an improvement?
options: Whenever the solution looks different
When evidence shows the result more closely meets the criterion
When the student prefers the change
Whenever a component is replaced
questions.correctFeedback: Improvement must be supported by comparison evidence rather than preference or the fact that a change occurred.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on whether the revised result performs better against the confirmed expectation.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; Lamp Idea Iteration, Drive ID 1OmW9UvXZ44MtOGNVmq7THl65bglDtKBwJ4exdkAqWF8; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Which sequence best represents controlled debugging?
options: Predict → test → record → compare → change one element → retest
Change everything → observe once → stop
Guess → replace parts → discard notes
Test without a criterion → choose a preferred result
questions.correctFeedback: Controlled debugging records evidence, isolates one change and retests against the same expectation.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the sequence that supports a traceable cause-and-effect investigation.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg

questions.question: What is evaluation?
options: A statement that the project is finished
A list of materials without explanation
A personal preference with no comparison
A reasoned judgement based on criteria and evidence
questions.correctFeedback: Evaluation connects a judgement with relevant evidence and a clear basis for comparison.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Look for the option that requires both evidence and reasoning.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: What does fitness for purpose consider?
options: Whether every design idea was manufactured
Whether the solution performs its intended purpose and meets relevant criteria
Whether the product uses the most materials
Whether the appearance matches another student’s work
questions.correctFeedback: Fitness for purpose is judged by comparing the solution’s performance with its intended purpose and criteria.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on how well the solution performs, not on quantity, imitation or unrelated features.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Which information is needed before making a reliable quality judgement?
options: A preferred design theme
A guessed performance threshold
Confirmed criteria and relevant evidence
Another student’s opinion
questions.correctFeedback: A valid judgement requires both an agreed expectation and evidence showing how the solution compares.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify the combination that allows a result to be checked fairly rather than assumed.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE

questions.question: Why should a sustainability judgement not rely only on the label “plantation”?
options: Plantations cannot produce timber
Plantation timber is always unsustainable
Labels are unrelated to forestry
Evidence about management, regeneration and impacts is still required
questions.correctFeedback: A forest category alone does not establish the full environmental, social and production effects.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider what additional evidence is needed before describing a timber source as sustainable.
questions.source: Timber Production worksheet, Drive ID 1dTRa-pimCafVnV_V7H0I16M_8Wn32-b7C_4NIXbfmaM; DAFF forestry glossary; ABARES Indicator 2.1b; TE4-SDP-01

questions.question: Which statement about native forests is supported?
options: They have ecological values requiring management and protection
All harvesting from them is harmful
They cannot provide any timber
Their products are always uncertified
questions.correctFeedback: Native forests support ecological systems, but their management effects must be judged from specific evidence.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Avoid absolute claims and identify the statement that recognises ecological value without assuming every outcome.
questions.source: Timber Production worksheet, Drive ID 1dTRa-pimCafVnV_V7H0I16M_8Wn32-b7C_4NIXbfmaM; ABARES Indicator 1.1a.i; TE4-SDP-01

questions.question: Which evidence would strengthen a sustainability judgement about the project timber?
options: Its colour alone
The word pine by itself
Its origin, management, regeneration and life-cycle impacts
An assumption that all plantations are identical
questions.correctFeedback: A strong sustainability judgement needs evidence about sourcing and effects over time.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose evidence that explains how the timber was produced and managed, not a label or appearance.
questions.source: Tools and Materials worksheet, Drive ID 1UnXP8FYDHNQsgOaRS036CZhLTCW9UXeoZC56gJbL2Tg; Timber Production worksheet, Drive ID 1dTRa-pimCafVnV_V7H0I16M_8Wn32-b7C_4NIXbfmaM

questions.question: What should a learning evaluation compare?
options: The lamp with an unrelated product
One student’s progress with another student’s result
The timber source with a coding algorithm
The student’s evidence with their personal goal
questions.correctFeedback: A learning evaluation uses evidence to judge progress against the student’s own goal and identify a next step.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Choose the comparison focused on personal development rather than unrelated work.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE

questions.question: How is a personal goal different from a project criterion?
options: A personal goal applies to every student’s product
A project criterion records one student’s improvement
A personal goal guides individual learning, while a criterion judges the solution
They must always use identical wording
questions.correctFeedback: These forms of evaluation have different subjects: student development and product performance.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Consider whether the statement is judging the learner or the designed solution.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: What does the reasoning part of claim-evidence-reasoning do?
options: Lists every material
Explains why the evidence supports the claim
Replaces the need for evidence
States a preference without justification
questions.correctFeedback: Reasoning explains the connection between the evidence and the judgement being made.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Identify the part that makes the logic behind the claim clear.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; TE4-DES-01

questions.question: Why should limitations be included in an evaluation?
options: To hide weaknesses in the evidence
To prove the project has failed
To avoid making any judgement
To show which conclusions cannot yet be fully supported
questions.correctFeedback: Acknowledging missing criteria or evidence makes the evaluation more accurate and trustworthy.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Focus on how identifying uncertainty prevents an evaluation from claiming more than the evidence supports.
questions.source: Unit Introduction and Success Criteria, Drive ID 1jABRQJb5uYOOPLWW-AG-mXDa3QEmGsUhoexCptn2aPE; Timber Production worksheet, Drive ID 1dTRa-pimCafVnV_V7H0I16M_8Wn32-b7C_4NIXbfmaM; TE4-DES-01
